triage.reason: Extremely common symptom with a critical differential from tension and migraine to subarachnoid hemorrhage; reachable by history and exam.

demographics: Tension-type headache is the most common primary headache and affects both sexes fairly equally
Migraine is about three times more common in women than men
Cluster headache is more common in men
Primary headache disorders often begin before age 40

risk_factors.text: Family history of migraine or other primary headache
Sustained neck or jaw strain (screen work, clenching)

family_history: Tension-type headache in a first-degree relative
exposures: Secondhand smoke or strong odors (migraine triggers)

chief_complaints.text: I get these headaches again and again
The pain is on one side and makes me sick to my stomach

hpi.onset: Usually gradual over 30 minutes to a few hours; migraine may build up, tension headache is often gradual, and a thunderclap onset is not typical of primary headache
hpi.duration: Episodes last 30 minutes to several hours for tension-type and 4–72 hours for migraine; cluster attacks last 15–180 minutes
hpi.progression: Recurrent episodes with a stable pattern over months to years; individual attacks build, plateau and then resolve
hpi.location: Tension-type: bilateral, band-like across the forehead, temples or back of the head; migraine: often unilateral, frontotemporal; cluster: strictly one-sided around the eye or temple
hpi.radiation: May spread from the neck and shoulders up into the head; migraine pain can spread across the whole head
hpi.quality: Tension-type: pressing or tightening, non-pulsating; migraine: throbbing or pulsating; cluster: sharp, boring, stabbing
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate for tension-type; moderate to severe for migraine; severe for cluster
hpi.timing: Tension-type is often constant through the day; migraine attacks are episodic; cluster attacks occur in bouts, often at the same time each day and at night
relieving: Resting in a dark, quiet room

associated_symptoms.text: Visual aura (flashing lights, zigzag lines, blind spots)
Tearing, red eye, runny nose or eyelid droop on one side (cluster)
Restlessness or pacing during the attack (cluster)

pertinent_negatives: Sudden severe headache reaching maximum in under a minute (thunderclap)
New confusion, weakness, numbness or trouble speaking
Headache that is worse when lying down or wakes from sleep
Painful red eye or vision loss
Weight loss, night sweats or known cancer

argues_against: Infection or malignancy as the cause

positives.text: Tearing or redness of one eye (cluster)
Runny or stuffy nose on one side (cluster)

negatives: Facial pressure worse when bending forward

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may not describe pain well and instead show irritability, crying, head-holding, vomiting or refusal to play; migraine attacks are often shorter than in adults.
New headache after age 50 is more concerning for secondary causes such as giant cell arteritis, mass lesion or medication overuse; migraine often becomes less severe with age.
New or worsening headache in pregnancy can signal preeclampsia or cerebral venous thrombosis, so blood pressure and neurologic red flags are checked carefully.
Headache may be the first sign of an opportunistic CNS infection or mass lesion, so fever, neck stiffness and focal deficits are weighed more heavily.

general.mild: Comfortable, alert, no distress; able to converse normally
general.moderate: Mild distress, prefers a dim quiet room, may squint or hold the head
general.severe: Marked distress, photophobic, nauseated, may be pacing or lying still depending on headache type
general.critical: Toxic or altered mental status, meningismus, focal deficit, or unable to cooperate with the exam

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation to person, place, time and situation; check attention and recall
findings.finding: Alert and fully oriented with normal cognition

findings.maneuver: Measure temperature and inspect for systemic signs of infection
findings.finding: Afebrile, no rash or systemic toxicity

findings.maneuver: Test cranial nerves II through XII, including visual fields, pupils, extraocular movements, facial strength and symmetry
findings.finding: Intact cranial nerve function with no ptosis, anisocoria, ophthalmoplegia or visual field cut

findings.maneuver: Test strength in all four limbs and light touch, pinprick and proprioception
findings.finding: Normal strength and sensation without focal deficit

findings.maneuver: Check deep tendon reflexes, finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin coordination, and gait including tandem walk
findings.finding: Symmetric reflexes, normal coordination and steady gait

findings.maneuver: Passively flex and rotate the neck, and perform Brudzinski and Kernig maneuvers
findings.finding: Full, painless neck range of motion without meningismus

findings.maneuver: Perform fundoscopy to assess the optic discs and venous pulsations
findings.finding: Sharp disc margins without papilledema and spontaneous venous pulsations present

findings.maneuver: Palpate the frontal and maxillary sinuses and transilluminate them
findings.finding: Facial tenderness or dullness over the sinuses

findings.maneuver: Palpate the temporal arteries for tenderness, nodularity and diminished pulsation
findings.finding: Tender, thickened or pulseless temporal artery

findings.maneuver: Palpate the temporalis and masseter muscles and ask the patient to clench the jaw
findings.finding: Tenderness or hypertrophy of the masticatory muscles

findings.maneuver: Palpate the pericranial muscles of the scalp, neck and shoulders
findings.finding: Tenderness or tightness of the pericranial and cervical muscles

findings.maneuver: Assess active and passive cervical range of motion
findings.finding: Reduced or painful cervical range of motion

findings.maneuver: Inspect the conjunctiva and eyelids for redness, tearing or ptosis
findings.finding: Unilateral conjunctival injection, lacrimation or eyelid edema

findings.maneuver: Inspect the nasal mucosa and turbinates
Auscultate the heart and lungs and check for carotid bruits
findings.finding: Regular rate and rhythm without murmur, rub or bruit; clear lungs

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen for tenderness, masses or organomegaly
Inspect the skin for rash, petechiae or lesions suggestive of systemic disease
findings.finding: No rash, petechiae or suspicious lesions

labs.caveat: Markedly elevated ESR (often over 50 mm/h) supports giant cell arteritis in a patient over 50 with new headache; a normal value does not fully exclude it.
Rises with giant cell arteritis and with infection; nonspecific on its own.
Leukocytosis with fever and meningismus points to meningitis or encephalitis rather than a primary headache.
Thrombocytopenia with headache and fever raises concern for a systemic infection or a hematologic process.
Hyponatremia can itself cause headache and altered mental status; also seen with SIADH from CNS infection or mass.
Hypoglycemia is a reversible cause of headache and confusion; check a bedside glucose in any patient with altered mental status.
Elevated opening pressure supports idiopathic intracranial hypertension, meningitis or a mass effect; measure before draining fluid.
Pleocytosis with fever and meningismus indicates meningitis; neutrophil predominance favors bacterial, lymphocyte predominance favors viral or other causes.
Elevated protein supports CNS infection or inflammation; very high values suggest bacterial meningitis or a block.
Low CSF glucose relative to serum favors bacterial or fungal meningitis; compare with a simultaneous serum glucose.
Xanthochromia suggests subarachnoid hemorrhage; cloudy fluid suggests infection.
Red cells that do not clear between tubes, or xanthochromia, point to subarachnoid hemorrhage rather than a traumatic tap.
Thyroid dysfunction can cause or worsen headache; check when the history suggests it.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or lumbar puncture; pregnancy also raises concern for preeclampsia and cerebral venous thrombosis.

imaging.preferred_when: First-line emergency imaging for red flags, trauma or suspected hemorrhage

findings.text: Subarachnoid blood in the basal cisterns or sulci
Mass lesion with surrounding edema and midline shift
Hyperdense dural venous sinus (suggesting venous thrombosis)

imaging.study: CT angiography of the head and neck
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected aneurysm, vascular malformation or dissection after a thunderclap headache

findings.text: Saccular aneurysm, most often at a branch point of the circle of Willis
Carotid or vertebral artery dissection with a narrowed lumen or intramural hematoma

imaging.study: MRI brain with and without IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Subacute or progressive headache, suspected mass, infection or demyelination

findings.text: White matter lesions consistent with demyelination
Empty sella, optic nerve sheath distension and transverse sinus narrowing (idiopathic intracranial hypertension)

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, especially in pregnancy or the postpartum period

findings.text: Filling defect in a dural venous sinus or cortical vein

imaging.preferred_when: Persistent concern for subarachnoid hemorrhage when the first CT was done more than 6 hours after onset

findings.text: Subarachnoid blood not seen on the earlier study

initial.why: Looks for infection, anemia or a hematologic process behind a secondary headache
Checks sodium, glucose and kidney function as reversible causes of headache and altered mental status

initial.only_if: new headache after age 50, especially with jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or visual symptoms

initial.why: Supports the ESR in suspected giant cell arteritis or infection
initial.only_if: new headache after age 50 or fever is present

initial.why: Rules out pregnancy before imaging or lumbar puncture
First-line emergency study for red flags, trauma or suspected hemorrhage
initial.only_if: any red flag is present: thunderclap onset, fever or meningismus, focal deficit, altered mental status, new headache after 50, head trauma, cancer or anticoagulation

confirmatory.why: Definitive test for subarachnoid hemorrhage when CT is negative or delayed, and for meningitis or encephalitis
confirmatory.only_if: suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage with a negative or late CT, or suspected CNS infection after imaging excludes a mass

confirmatory.test: CT angiography of the head and neck
confirmatory.why: Identifies an aneurysm, vascular malformation or dissection after a thunderclap headache
confirmatory.only_if: thunderclap headache with a negative CT and lumbar puncture, or focal vascular symptoms

confirmatory.test: MRI brain with and without IV contrast
confirmatory.why: Best study for a mass, infection, demyelination or idiopathic intracranial hypertension
confirmatory.only_if: progressive or subacute headache, focal findings, or a normal CT that does not explain the presentation
suspected venous thrombosis, especially in pregnancy or the postpartum period

supporting.why: Thyroid dysfunction can cause or worsen headache
Elevated opening pressure supports idiopathic intracranial hypertension or meningitis
Xanthochromia suggests subarachnoid hemorrhage and cloudiness suggests infection
Pleocytosis indicates CNS infection or inflammation
Elevated protein supports CNS infection or inflammation
Low CSF glucose favors bacterial or fungal meningitis

not_indicated.why: Not needed for a stable, recurrent primary headache with a normal neurologic exam and no red flags

not_indicated.test: MRI brain with and without IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not a routine test for typical migraine or tension-type headache
Not indicated without suspicion of hemorrhage or CNS infection
No role in headache unless cerebral venous thrombosis is suspected
Not needed unless abdominal pain is present
Not part of the headache workup unless urinary symptoms are present

decision_points: Any red flag (thunderclap onset, fever or meningismus, focal deficit, altered mental status, new headache after 50, head trauma, cancer, anticoagulation, papilledema) moves the patient from a primary headache pathway to urgent imaging
Pregnancy test before CT or lumbar puncture in anyone who could be pregnant
CT first for suspected hemorrhage; lumbar puncture if CT is negative or was done more than 6 hours after onset
Start empiric antibiotics and antivirals before lumbar puncture when bacterial meningitis is suspected and imaging must come first
Check a bedside glucose in any patient with headache and altered mental status

differential.name: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
differential.why_considered: Headache is the cardinal symptom, and a benign-appearing headache can be the only warning before a catastrophic rebleed.
differential.trigger: Thunderclap onset reaching maximum intensity within seconds to a minute, or headache with meningismus, vomiting or transient loss of consciousness

history: Sudden severe headache that peaks in under a minute
Vomiting at onset
Brief loss of consciousness or a sentinel headache days earlier
No prior identical headache pattern
exam: Altered mental status or focal deficit
Papilledema or retinal hemorrhage on fundoscopy
labs: Xanthochromic CSF that does not clear between tubes
imaging: Subarachnoid blood in the basal cisterns or sulci on non-contrast CT
Aneurysm at a circle of Willis branch point on CT angiography
Blood not seen on a CT done more than 6 hours after onset, requiring lumbar puncture

differential.name: Bacterial meningitis
differential.why_considered: Headache with fever and neck stiffness is the classic triad and can progress to sepsis and death within hours.
differential.trigger: Fever with headache and neck stiffness, especially with altered mental status, rash or recent infection

history: Fever and chills
Rapid progression over hours
Recent ear, sinus or bloodstream infection
Unvaccinated or immunocompromised state
exam: Nuchal rigidity with positive Brudzinski or Kernig sign
Focal neurologic deficit or cranial nerve palsy
labs: Elevated CSF white cell count with neutrophil predominance
Elevated CSF protein and low CSF glucose
imaging: CT head first only to exclude a mass before lumbar puncture when focal deficits or altered mental status are present

differential.name: Migraine
differential.why_considered: The most common cause of recurrent moderate to severe headache with nausea and light sensitivity.

history: Recurrent attacks with an identical pattern over months to years
Unilateral throbbing pain lasting 4 to 72 hours
Nausea with light and sound sensitivity
Visual aura before the pain
Aggravated by routine physical activity
exam: Patient prefers a dark, quiet room during the attack
No fever, meningismus or focal deficit
imaging: Normal CT or MRI; imaging not required for typical migraine

differential.name: Tension-type headache
differential.why_considered: The most common primary headache, with bilateral pressing pain and neck or shoulder tightness.

history: Bilateral, band-like pressing or tightening pain
Mild to moderate severity without vomiting
No aura and no aggravation by routine activity
Often related to stress, poor sleep or skipped meals
exam: Tenderness of pericranial, neck and shoulder muscles
imaging: Normal CT or MRI; imaging not required

differential.name: Cluster headache
differential.why_considered: Severe strictly unilateral periorbital pain with autonomic features, often mistaken for a sinus or eye problem.

history: Severe one-sided pain around the eye or temple lasting 15 to 180 minutes
Attacks in bouts, often at the same time each day and waking the patient at night
Restlessness or pacing during the attack
More common in men and associated with alcohol triggers
exam: Unilateral conjunctival injection, tearing or eyelid edema
Ptosis or miosis on the affected side
imaging: Normal brain MRI; imaging is used to exclude a secondary cause of a cluster-like headache

differential.name: Giant cell arteritis
differential.why_considered: New headache in an older adult that can cause irreversible vision loss if not treated promptly.
differential.trigger: New headache after age 50, especially with jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or visual symptoms

history: New headache after age 50
Jaw claudication with chewing
Scalp tenderness when brushing hair
Transient or permanent visual loss
Constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss and malaise
exam: Tender, thickened or pulseless temporal artery
Visual field defect or decreased visual acuity
labs: Markedly elevated ESR, often over 50 mm/h
imaging: Temporal artery biopsy showing vasculitis is the confirmatory test
Vascular ultrasound or MRI showing temporal artery wall thickening or halo sign

differential.name: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
differential.why_considered: Headache with papilledema in a young woman with obesity, without a mass lesion.

history: Daily or positional headache worse lying down or on waking
Transient visual obscurations
Pulsatile tinnitus
Young woman with obesity or recent weight gain
exam: Enlarged blind spot or visual field defect
Normal mental status and no focal deficit
labs: Elevated CSF opening pressure with normal CSF cell count, protein and glucose
imaging: Empty sella, optic nerve sheath distension and transverse sinus narrowing on MRI
No mass lesion or hydrocephalus on imaging

differential.name: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
differential.why_considered: Severe headache with eye pain and visual change that can cause permanent vision loss if missed.
differential.trigger: Painful red eye with headache, blurred vision or halos around lights

history: Severe eye pain with headache
Blurred vision or halos around lights
Nausea and vomiting
Recent dim light exposure or anticholinergic medication
exam: Red eye with a fixed mid-dilated pupil
imaging: Elevated intraocular pressure on tonometry is the key finding
Shallow anterior chamber on slit-lamp examination

differential.name: Acute sinusitis
differential.why_considered: Facial pain and pressure with headache, often mistaken for migraine or tension-type headache.

history: Facial pressure or pain worse when bending forward
Purulent nasal discharge
Recent upper respiratory infection
Fever and malaise
exam: Tenderness over the frontal or maxillary sinuses
Purulent nasal discharge or mucosal edema
imaging: Sinus opacification or air-fluid level on CT, reserved for complicated or atypical cases

differential.name: Medication overuse headache
differential.why_considered: Daily or near-daily headache in a patient taking pain relievers frequently, often mistaken for worsening primary headache.

history: Headache on 15 or more days per month
Regular use of acetaminophen, NSAIDs, triptans or opioids for headache
Headache improves briefly after each dose then returns
History of migraine or tension-type headache
imaging: Normal CT or MRI; imaging not required

severity.mild: Intermittent, mild to moderate headache that does not limit activity; normal neurologic exam; no red flags; responds to rest or over-the-counter pain relievers
severity.moderate: Moderate to severe headache with nausea, light or sound sensitivity, or functional limitation; normal neurologic exam; no red flags; may need prescription therapy
severity.severe: Severe disabling headache with vomiting, marked photophobia or phonophobia, or inability to function; normal neurologic exam; no red flags; requires urgent evaluation and parenteral therapy
severity.critical: Headache with any red flag: thunderclap onset, fever or meningismus, focal deficit, altered mental status, papilledema, new headache after age 50, head trauma, cancer or anticoagulation; requires immediate imaging and possible lumbar puncture

red_flags.finding: Thunderclap onset reaching maximum intensity within seconds to a minute
red_flags.meaning: Subarachnoid hemorrhage until proven otherwise; obtain urgent non-contrast CT head and lumbar puncture or CT angiography

red_flags.finding: Fever with neck stiffness or meningismus
red_flags.meaning: Meningitis or encephalitis; start empiric antibiotics and antivirals after blood cultures and before lumbar puncture when imaging must come first

red_flags.finding: New focal neurologic deficit, weakness, numbness or trouble speaking
red_flags.meaning: Stroke, mass lesion or CNS infection; obtain urgent imaging

red_flags.finding: Altered mental status or new confusion
red_flags.meaning: CNS infection, hemorrhage, mass lesion or metabolic cause; check bedside glucose and obtain urgent imaging
Raised intracranial pressure from a mass, venous thrombosis or idiopathic intracranial hypertension; obtain urgent imaging before lumbar puncture
Giant cell arteritis, mass lesion or medication overuse; check ESR and CRP and consider temporal artery biopsy
Intracranial hemorrhage; obtain urgent non-contrast CT head

red_flags.finding: Known cancer or anticoagulation with new headache
red_flags.meaning: Metastatic disease or intracranial hemorrhage; obtain urgent imaging

red_flags.finding: Painful red eye with visual change
red_flags.meaning: Acute angle-closure glaucoma; check intraocular pressure urgently

red_flags.finding: Headache worse when lying down or waking the patient from sleep
red_flags.meaning: Raised intracranial pressure or mass lesion; obtain imaging

red_flags.finding: Progressive worsening over weeks with weight loss or night sweats
red_flags.meaning: Malignancy or chronic infection; obtain imaging and systemic workup

complications.name: Disability and lost productivity from chronic headache
Medication overuse headache
clues: Headache on 15 or more days per month
Regular use of acute pain relievers

complications.name: Progression to chronic migraine
clues: Headache on 15 or more days per month for more than 3 months

complications.name: Rebleeding from a ruptured aneurysm
clues: New focal deficit or loss of consciousness

complications.name: Cerebral edema, herniation or death from raised intracranial pressure
clues: New focal deficit or pupillary asymmetry

complications.name: Permanent vision loss from giant cell arteritis or acute angle-closure glaucoma

special_populations.differences: Young children may not describe pain well and instead show irritability, crying, head-holding, vomiting or refusal to play; migraine attacks are often shorter than in adults and may be accompanied by abdominal symptoms.
New headache after age 50 is more concerning for giant cell arteritis, mass lesion or medication overuse; migraine often becomes less severe with age and may lose its aura.
New or worsening headache in pregnancy or the postpartum period can signal preeclampsia or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis; check blood pressure, urine protein and consider MR venography.
Headache may be the first sign of an opportunistic CNS infection or mass lesion; fever, neck stiffness and focal deficits are weighed more heavily and imaging is obtained earlier.

key_questions.question: How did the headache start — suddenly or gradually?
key_questions.looking_for: Thunderclap onset reaching maximum intensity within seconds to a minute suggests subarachnoid hemorrhage; gradual onset over 30 minutes to hours fits a primary headache

key_questions.question: When did it start, and how long does each episode last?
key_questions.looking_for: Tension-type 30 minutes to several hours; migraine 4 to 72 hours; cluster 15 to 180 minutes; a new pattern over days to weeks suggests a secondary cause

key_questions.question: Where is the pain, and what does it feel like?
key_questions.looking_for: Bilateral band-like pressing pain favors tension-type; unilateral throbbing favors migraine; strictly one-sided periorbital sharp pain favors cluster

key_questions.question: How severe is it, and does it limit what you can do?
key_questions.looking_for: Mild to moderate without activity limitation favors tension-type; moderate to severe with disability favors migraine; severe with restlessness favors cluster

key_questions.question: What makes it worse or better?
key_questions.looking_for: Aggravation by routine physical activity, light or noise favors migraine; relief with rest in a dark quiet room favors migraine; no clear triggers favors tension-type

key_questions.question: Do you have nausea, vomiting, or sensitivity to light or sound?
key_questions.looking_for: Nausea with photophobia and phonophobia supports migraine; vomiting at onset with meningismus raises concern for subarachnoid hemorrhage or meningitis

key_questions.question: Do you get any warning before the pain, such as flashing lights or zigzag lines?
key_questions.looking_for: Visual aura before the pain supports migraine with aura

key_questions.question: Do you have tearing, redness of one eye, runny nose, or a droopy eyelid with the attacks?
key_questions.looking_for: Unilateral cranial autonomic features support cluster headache

key_questions.question: Do you have fever, neck stiffness, confusion, weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking?
key_questions.looking_for: Any of these moves the patient to an urgent secondary-headache pathway for meningitis, encephalitis, hemorrhage or stroke

key_questions.question: Have you had a head injury, or are you on blood thinners?
key_questions.looking_for: Head trauma or anticoagulation raises concern for intracranial hemorrhage and warrants urgent imaging

key_questions.question: Is this a new headache pattern for you, or the same as your usual headaches?
key_questions.looking_for: A new or changed pattern, especially after age 50, raises concern for a secondary cause such as giant cell arteritis or a mass lesion

key_questions.question: How often do you take pain relievers for your headaches?
key_questions.looking_for: Frequent use of acetaminophen, NSAIDs, triptans or opioids on 15 or more days per month suggests medication overuse headache

key_questions.question: Have you had headaches like this before, and does anyone in your family get migraines?
key_questions.looking_for: A long-standing recurrent pattern with a family history of migraine supports a primary headache disorder

key_questions.question: How much sleep are you getting, and are you skipping meals or under a lot of stress?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor sleep, skipped meals, dehydration and stress are common triggers for tension-type headache and migraine

key_questions.question: Do you have jaw pain when chewing, scalp tenderness, or any change in vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or visual symptoms in a patient over 50 suggest giant cell arteritis and risk of permanent vision loss

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy raises concern for preeclampsia and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and must be excluded before imaging or lumbar puncture

reasoning_points: Characterizes the headache by onset, duration, location, quality, severity, timing, aggravating and relieving factors
Distinguishes a primary headache disorder from a secondary cause using the presence or absence of red flags

Identifies thunderclap onset, fever with meningismus, focal deficit, altered mental status, papilledema, new headache after age 50, head trauma, cancer or anticoagulation as red flags requiring urgent imaging
Recognizes the pattern of migraine: recurrent unilateral throbbing pain lasting 4 to 72 hours with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia, aggravated by routine activity
Recognizes the pattern of tension-type headache: bilateral pressing pain, mild to moderate, without vomiting or activity aggravation
Recognizes the pattern of cluster headache: severe strictly unilateral periorbital pain lasting 15 to 180 minutes with ipsilateral autonomic features and restlessness
Considers medication overuse headache when headaches occur on 15 or more days per month with frequent analgesic use
Considers giant cell arteritis in a patient over 50 with new headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or visual symptoms and checks ESR and CRP
Considers acute angle-closure glaucoma when headache is accompanied by a painful red eye and visual change
Documents a complete neurologic exam including mental status, cranial nerves, motor, sensory, coordination, gait and fundoscopy
Orders a pregnancy test before imaging or lumbar puncture in anyone who could be pregnant
Avoids routine imaging in a stable, recurrent primary headache with a normal neurologic exam and no red flags

easy: Young woman with recurrent unilateral throbbing headache, nausea and light sensitivity consistent with migraine
Bilateral band-like pressing headache with neck and shoulder tightness and no red flags consistent with tension-type headache
Long-standing stable pattern with a normal neurologic exam
medium: Severe one-sided periorbital pain with tearing and nasal congestion consistent with cluster headache
Daily headache with frequent analgesic use consistent with medication overuse headache
Facial pressure and purulent nasal discharge consistent with acute sinusitis
Headache with visual aura that must be distinguished from transient ischemic attack
hard: Thunderclap headache with a normal neurologic exam that requires CT and lumbar puncture to exclude subarachnoid hemorrhage
New headache after age 50 with jaw claudication and elevated ESR consistent with giant cell arteritis
Headache with papilledema in a young woman with obesity consistent with idiopathic intracranial hypertension
Headache with a painful red eye and halos consistent with acute angle-closure glaucoma
Headache in pregnancy or the postpartum period raising concern for preeclampsia or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
Child with irritability, vomiting and head-holding who cannot describe the pain
